beats.narration_text: A raccoon just wants a quiet night in his tree. Then a party starts right underneath it. I'm Abhinav, and this is The Noise Next Door, the game I'm finishing as my final project. Everything you see playing is real play. When something isn't built yet, I'll say so.

beats.narration_text: It's a slapstick stealth-puzzle game for desktop. You pester the campers under your tree, get chased into town in a camper's red beanie, and get driven home by that same camper. Level one now runs end to end, from the title screen to the chase out of the camp. The city, the block and the ride home are still to build. Finished, it's a game you play from title screen to end screen, on Windows or a Mac.

beats.narration_text: Level one ends like this. Five jobs in, the camper brings out a cake, and the whole camp gathers round. I tie his laces, he trips, the cake lands on his face, and I grab his red beanie. Then the men chase me out, and the moth leads the way.

beats.narration_text: Why would anyone care? You're the pest, not the hero, and every job comes from reading the campers. Spotted, I hop into the keeper's box, and they lose me. They search right round it, so I burst out and scare them. The worst they can do is shoo me off: no health, no lives, no game over.

beats.narration_text: What does the player get? The sneaky fun of a heist at night. When a camper spots me, I dive into a bush and they lose me. Their sight is drawn on the ground, and it shrinks while I sneak. And when a job lands, it's crossed off the list.

beats.narration_text: What's different? I've played Untitled Goose Game and Stray. Goose Game makes you the pest too, working down a to-do list, but you can't see who's watching. Here you can, so you plan the job around it. Stray puts a cat in a city whose people are gone. Here, the people are the puzzle.

beats.narration_text: Who opens it? I'm aiming at gameplay programmer roles, so it's for a hiring manager or a lead. They'll open the build on Windows or a Mac. This is what they'd get today, from New Game: a moth flies ahead of him down the trail to the party, with one task on screen. A lead can also rerun every test, one command each.

beats.narration_text: What does it prove? In October my design document said the game had no humans yet. Now it has four, with routines and sight. Shaders, particles, and the jump's animation are each built and tested, with headless tests a stranger can rerun. What it can't prove yet is whether people enjoy it. Nobody outside the project has played it.

beats.narration_text: What's in, what's out, and what's first? Out: save states. My design document plans them, and I'm cutting them so the game plays in one sitting. First: level one exported for Windows and macOS, with a headless test that plays it from New Game to the chase out of the camp. That test will show it ran, and so will the Windows build, outside the editor. I don't have a Mac, so the Mac build stays untested.

beats.narration_text: What could sink it? Scope. It's three levels for one person, and level one alone has taken about a month. The town needs a cast that doesn't exist yet: three dogs, an animal-control officer, the neighbours. So level one gets finished and exported first, and each new level starts only once the last one exports and passes its tests.

beats.narration_text: Why this project? Mostly to learn. Godot, Blender modelling and rigging, shaders, particles, and game animation with its tests were all new to me this term, and I've used every one of them in this game. Finishing this game is how I'll find out whether I can carry them all through to the end.
